articles.title: What They Left Off the Table
articles.dek: A family quietly left something off the fiesta spread for one friend's sake — and Paul's letter to a food-obsessed church in Corinth explains why that's the most mature thing love can do.
articles.quote: Love always asks a better question than "Am I allowed?" It asks, "What will this cost the person watching me?"
articles.illustration: family skips alcohol at fiesta for Jun
articles.body:
On the night of the fiesta, the table groaned with lechon, pancit, kilawin, and the good cousin's lechon manok. But if you looked closely at the ice chest by the door, something was missing. No San Miguel. No tuba. Not one bottle of anything that could get a person drunk. Nobody made an announcement about it. The tita who usually brought the Red Horse just didn't bring it that year. Everyone understood without being told: Jun was coming, fresh out of nine months of getting sober, and this was his first fiesta back among people who used to hand him a bottle before he even sat down.

Nobody thought drinking was a sin. Half the people at that table would have a beer at the next barangay basketball game without a second thought. But that night, for that table, they laid it down. Not because the thing itself was wrong, but because someone they loved was still learning to say no, and none of them wanted their yes to be the reason he fell. This happens more often than we notice, in barangays all over the Philippines — a quiet, unspoken decision to give up something harmless for the sake of someone who isn't strong enough yet to be around it. It rarely makes the news. But it is one of the most Christian things a family can do, whether they know it or not, because it is almost exactly the argument the apostle Paul makes to a church very far away, about a food fight that was tearing them apart.

Corinth was a city built on trade and stone and appetite. Merchant ships came through its two harbors carrying silver, silk, and worshippers of a dozen gods, and the city answered with temples — to Aphrodite, to Apollo, to Asclepius the healer — set right into its hillsides and marketplaces. Here is the detail most people miss: almost every piece of meat sold in Corinth's public market had, at some point, passed through one of those temples. An animal was brought in, a portion burned on the altar, a portion kept by the priests, and the rest sold off in the meat market to make room for the next sacrifice. Archaeologists have even found dining rooms built directly into temple courtyards, where Corinthians held wedding banquets, business dinners, and guild meetings — with meat from the very altar a few steps away. If you wanted lamb for Sunday dinner in Corinth, you could barely avoid a god's fingerprints on it.

So when people became Christians in Corinth, a real question landed on their plates: can I eat this? Some believers — clearly the ones with more education, more standing, more comfort in their new faith — had already worked out the answer. "We know that 'An idol is nothing at all in the world,'" they said, quoting what sounds like their own church slogan back at Paul, "and that there is no God but one" (1 Corinthians 8:4). If the god behind the statue doesn't exist, then meat offered to it is just meat. No magic in it, no curse on it. Eat it at a friend's wedding, eat it at your business partner's table, eat it without flinching. Paul does not argue with the theology. He agrees with it completely.

But not everyone in that church had the same history. Some of them had, until very recently, actually believed in that god. They had bowed at that altar, feared that idol, built a life around appeasing it. Paul calls this their "conscience" being "weak" — not weak in courage, but untrained, still tender, not yet able to see the meat as just meat (8:7). And here is where the danger showed up: if one of these new believers saw a respected, "strong" Christian eating comfortably inside an idol's temple dining room, what would they conclude? Not "meat is neutral." They would conclude something far more dangerous — that it must be safe to go back, to sit at that table again, to test the old god one more time. And a heart that fragile, pulled back toward something it had only just escaped, could come undone. Paul does not treat this lightly. He says the weak brother, seeing this, is "destroyed" by the very knowledge the strong believer was so proud of (8:11).

"Be careful, however, that the exercise of your rights does not become a stumbling block to the weak." (1 Corinthians 8:9, NIV)

Notice what Paul does not say. He does not say the strong believers are wrong about the idol. He does not say they should suddenly start being afraid of statues. He says something more searching: being right was never the finish line. "Knowledge puffs up," he writes, "while love builds up" (8:1). Knowledge can tell you exactly what you're allowed to do. It cannot, by itself, tell you what love requires you to lay down. Those are two different questions, and the Corinthians who prided themselves on the first question had stopped asking the second one entirely.

It's worth sitting with the reason Paul gives, because it isn't "because rules are rules." It's this: "So this weak brother or sister, for whom Christ died, is destroyed by your knowledge" (8:11). For whom Christ died. Paul measures the weight of that other person not by how mature their faith is, not by how much theology they've absorbed, but by what it cost God to have them at all. You can win every argument about idol meat and still trample over someone Jesus bled for. That reframes the whole question. It's no longer "am I allowed to do this." It's "what will this cost the person watching me do it."

That is why Paul ends the chapter the way he does — not with a rule for everyone, but with a resolve for himself: "if what I eat causes my brother or sister to fall into sin, I will never eat meat again, so that I will not cause them to fall" (8:13). He isn't laying down a law. He's showing what love looks like when it takes another person's fragility seriously enough to change its own habits for them.

Most of us will never argue about meat sacrificed to idols. But the shape of this problem shows up constantly. It's the friend group that keeps the drinks flowing in front of someone newly sober. It's the jokes about sabong or online betting tossed around a table where someone is quietly climbing out of gambling debt. It's flaunting a purchase, a vacation, a freedom, in front of someone still healing from the very thing that freedom resembles. None of those things may be wrong in themselves. That was never really the question. The question Paul keeps asking is who is at the table, what they're still carrying, and whether your freedom is worth more to you than they are.

That family who quietly left the alcohol off the fiesta table never wrote a theology paper about it. They didn't need to. They understood, in their bones, the same thing Paul was teaching a church three thousand kilometers and two thousand years away: love always asks a better question than "Am I allowed?" It asks, "What will this cost the person watching me?"

So here is something to carry into today, and maybe into your next fiesta, your next reunion, your next ordinary Tuesday dinner. Look around the table. Someone there may be carrying something you can't see — a fragile sobriety, a new faith, a wound still healing. You don't have to change who you are for them forever. You just have to love them enough, tonight, to lay one small thing down. That's not weakness. Paul would call it the most mature thing at the table.

articles.title: Eyes for the Blind, Feet for the Lame
articles.dek: Job's most cherished memory wasn't his wealth — it was the widows, strangers, and orphans he'd stood up for. A stockbroker who quietly saved hundreds of children discovered the same wisdom decades later, in an attic scrapbook.
articles.quote: Job's greatness, in his own retelling, is not a thing he possessed. It is a list of people who were better off because he existed.
articles.body:
On a December evening in 1988, a retired London stockbroker named Nicholas Winton sat in the front row of a BBC television studio, invited by his wife to what he thought was just another taping. The host, Esther Rantzen, held up an old scrapbook and began reading names and photographs from it, a list of children Winton had quietly arranged safe passage for out of Nazi-occupied Czechoslovakia in 1939, nearly six hundred of them, on trains he organized himself, paid for himself, and never told anyone about for almost fifty years. Then Rantzen asked a simple question to the studio audience: is there anyone here tonight who owes their life to Nicholas Winton? Winton turned around. Every single person in the row behind him stood up. He had not known a single one of their faces. He had saved their lives as infants and toddlers and never expected to meet the grown versions of them, let alone be seated among them by accident.

Winton never called it heroism. He was a stockbroker who happened to be good at paperwork, patient with bureaucracies, and unwilling to look away from a problem he could actually fix. He spent his evenings after work finding foster families, forging visa approvals when the real ones moved too slowly, and writing hundreds of letters, one child at a time, until the last train he arranged never made it out because war broke out the next day. Then he put the scrapbook in his attic and moved on with an ordinary life, until his wife found it decades later while cleaning.

Job, in chapter 29, is also going through an old scrapbook. He is sitting in ashes, covered in sores, having just endured chapter after chapter of friends telling him his suffering must be punishment for some hidden sin. And in the middle of that grief, his mind drifts back, not to his wealth, not to his health, but to the days when "God's intimate friendship blessed my house" (Job 29:4). He remembers what his life used to look like from the outside, through the eyes of the people he helped.

What follows is one of the most tender self-portraits in the whole Bible. Job recalls walking into the city gate, the place where the elders gathered and disputes were settled, and how young men stepped aside and old men rose to their feet when he arrived. Not because he demanded it. Because of what he had done for them. "Whoever heard me spoke well of me, and those who saw me commended me," he says, "because I rescued the poor who cried for help, and the fatherless who had none to assist them. The one who was dying blessed me; I made the widow's heart sing" (Job 29:11-13). Then comes the line that reads like it was lifted straight out of Winton's story before Winton was ever born.

"I was eyes to the blind and feet to the lame. I was a father to the needy; I took up the case of the stranger." (Job 29:15-16)

Notice what Job does not list as his legacy. He does not say, "I had the most livestock in the East" or "everyone respected how smart I was." His proudest memory is entirely relational. He was someone else's eyes. Someone else's feet. Someone else's father when their own was gone. Someone else's lawyer when no one would take their case. Job's greatness, in his own retelling, is not a thing he possessed. It is a list of people who were better off because he existed.

That is worth sitting with for a moment, especially next to the famous question one chapter earlier: "Where can wisdom be found? Where does understanding dwell?" (Job 28:12). Chapter 28 is a small masterpiece on its own, a poem about miners tunneling into mountains, overturning rock in search of silver and gold and sapphires, going further into the dark than any bird has flown or lion has prowled, and still coming up empty-handed, because wisdom is not a vein of ore. It cannot be purchased, weighed, or mined. The chapter ends with the only answer that satisfies: "The fear of the Lord—that is wisdom, and to shun evil is understanding" (Job 28:28).

Read Job 28 and Job 29 side by side and something clicks. Chapter 28 asks the question in the abstract. Chapter 29 answers it in the concrete. Job never found wisdom by digging. He found it, or rather lived it, by becoming eyes for someone who had none. Real wisdom, the kind no mine can produce, kept showing up in his life as ordinary, unglamorous rescue: a widow's case taken up, a stranger's cause defended, a dying man comforted before the end. Winton never read Job 28, as far as we know, but he stumbled onto the same answer from the opposite direction. He didn't go looking for wisdom in a library. He found it in a stack of visa forms and a willingness to keep writing letters after everyone else had given up.

There is an ache underneath Job's memory that we shouldn't rush past. He is not bragging here; he is grieving. Everything he describes in chapter 29 is gone by the time he says it, and the chapters right after this one describe how far he has fallen, how the same young men who once stepped aside now mock him. Job's wisdom didn't protect him from suffering. It's worth noticing that anyway, because it means the value of what he did in chapter 29 was never contingent on what came after in chapter 30. The widow's heart still sang. The stranger's case still got heard. Those rescues stayed true even after everything else Job had was stripped away, and that says something important about the kind of wisdom that matters: it doesn't need to be permanent to be worth everything.

So here is a question worth carrying into today, the same one Winton's scrapbook quietly asks and Job's memory answers without meaning to: whose case is sitting in front of you right now, unclaimed? It rarely announces itself as a grand cause. It looks like a coworker nobody defends in the meeting, an elderly neighbor who needs someone to read the fine print on a bill, a stranger's kid who could use one adult who shows up consistently. You do not need a title, a mine full of silver, or fifty years of hindsight to be somebody's eyes and somebody's feet today. Job's finest chapter wasn't the one where he had the most. It was the one where he mattered most to people who had the least. That is a legacy still open for the taking, starting this afternoon.

articles.title: The Candles That Couldn't Hold Stones
articles.dek: For seven quiet years, a small prayer meeting in Leipzig sang as if their enemies had already lost, long before anyone could prove it. Psalm 92 says that's not wishful thinking, it's worship.
articles.quote: My eyes have seen isn't hindsight — it's eyesight trained by worship, learning to see the ending before it arrives.
articles.body:
In September 1982, a small group started gathering every Monday evening at five o'clock in St. Nicholas Church in Leipzig, East Germany. They called it a peace prayer. There were maybe twenty of them at first, sitting in a building that could seat two thousand, praying quietly in a country that recorded who came and went. The Stasi, East Germany's secret police, took notes. Agents sat in the pews. Informants counted faces at the door and filed names into cabinets that would eventually hold six million dossiers on the country's own citizens. Nothing visible changed. Not that Monday, not the next one, not for years.

They kept coming anyway. The group grew slowly — thirty, then a hundred, then a few hundred — always the same quiet order of service: a reading, a hymn, a prayer for the very people watching them, and then everyone went home to ordinary Tuesdays. For seven years, that was the whole story. A small church. A modest crowd. A government with tanks, prisons, and no apparent plans to move an inch.

Then came October 9, 1989. Word had spread that the army had live ammunition ready and hospitals had cleared beds, bracing for what officials privately called "a Chinese solution" — a crackdown like the one in Tiananmen Square four months earlier. Roughly seventy thousand people filled the church, the square outside, and the streets beyond it that night. When the service ended, they walked out into the dark in complete silence, each one carrying a lit candle, cupping the flame with both hands to keep it from going out. A hand wrapped carefully around a candle cannot also hold a stone. The security forces, ordered to be ready for anything, watched thousands of unarmed people stream past them singing hymns — and did not fire a single shot. Five weeks later, the Berlin Wall opened for good, and a government that had stood for forty years came apart without a single window broken by that crowd.

Psalm 92 was written centuries earlier and half a world away, but it knows exactly what those seven quiet years felt like. It's a Sabbath song — meant to be sung on the one day each week set aside for rest — and it doesn't pretend evil isn't real or that it loses quickly. A few verses before our passage, the psalmist admits plainly that "the wicked spring up like grass and all evildoers flourish" (Psalm 92:7). He isn't writing from safety on the other side of trouble. He's writing from inside a world where the people doing wrong still seem, for now, to be winning. And then, with nothing in his circumstances having changed, he says this:

"You have exalted my horn like that of a wild ox; fine oils have been poured on me. My eyes have seen the defeat of my adversaries; my ears have heard the rout of my wicked foes." (Psalm 92:10–11, NIV)

Read that again, slowly. "My eyes have seen." Not "my eyes will see one day." Not "I hope my eyes will see." He speaks of his enemies' defeat as something already witnessed — in the past tense — while, by his own admission two verses earlier, those same enemies are still flourishing like grass in springtime. It's worth sitting with what that means: the psalmist isn't reporting news that already broke. He's declaring a verdict before the evidence has fully arrived.

That's exactly what a candle at a Monday prayer meeting is. It isn't proof the wall is coming down. It's a small, stubborn act of worship that speaks as if it already has. The horn of the wild ox, lifted high, was an ancient picture of strength and dignity restored — the opposite of a bowed head or a hidden face. The fine oil poured out was for refreshment, the kind of ordinary comfort you'd offer an honored guest at the end of a long, hard day. Neither image required the enemy to already be gone. Both were things the psalmist let God do in him while the outcome was still unseen — a lifted head and a refreshed spirit, worn like clothes he put on before the day earned them. Notice, too, that he never explains how or when his adversaries will fall. The psalm doesn't hand him a timeline. It hands him a posture.

Here's the part easy to miss on a quick read: verse 11 isn't hindsight. It's eyesight trained by worship. The people who kept gathering in that church for seven years weren't waiting to sing until they had something to sing about. The singing itself was how they kept seeing an ending that hadn't come yet. By the time seventy thousand candles lit that October night, they had already been rehearsing, Monday after Monday, what it would feel like to watch their adversaries' plans come to nothing. My eyes have seen isn't hindsight — it's eyesight trained by worship, learning to see the ending before it arrives.

Maybe you're carrying something similar right now — a situation at work that seems stacked unfairly against you, a health report you're still waiting on, a relationship that's been cold for so long you've stopped expecting warmth from it, a wrong done to you or someone you love that has never once been made right. The wicked, as the psalm bluntly puts it, are still springing up like grass in your life too. It would be easy to wait for the visible ending before you let your shoulders come down, before you let your own voice sound like someone who already knows how the story turns out. It's a very human instinct — to keep score in silence, waiting until the numbers are official before allowing yourself any relief.

Psalm 92 offers a quieter, sturdier way, one within reach on any ordinary evening — no crowd of seventy thousand required. Bring your hands together the way those churchgoers did: not empty, and not full of stones, but cupped around something small and lit. A prayer spoken as though it's already answered. A hymn hummed under your breath on a Tuesday when nothing outward has changed yet. Gratitude offered before the circumstances have earned it. None of this pretends the hard thing isn't hard. It simply lets worship walk ahead of your circumstances and lend your eyes something to see before they're allowed to see it on their own.

Tonight, or whenever your own version of a Monday comes around, try saying it the way the psalmist did — not "I hope this ends well" but, quietly, even if only to yourself, "my eyes have seen it end well." You may be surprised how much steadier your hands feel, holding a small light instead of just waiting for one to appear.

articles.title: The Season That Doesn't Wait
articles.dek: A squirrel's frantic autumn scramble reveals something Solomon already knew — and it has nothing to do with hoarding.
articles.quote: Diligence isn't anxious hustle. It's paying loving attention to the moment God has actually given you.
articles.body:
Every October, a gray squirrel does something that looks like panic but isn't. It buries as many as ten thousand nuts, one at a time, across dozens of separate locations — a tree root here, a flowerbed there, a gap under a porch step three yards away. Researchers who study this behavior, including a well-known series of experiments at UC Berkeley, discovered something the squirrels never advertise: this isn't random burying. The squirrels sort as they go. They cluster acorns by species, by size, by how soon each nut will spoil, building a kind of mental map organized by category, not just location. Months later, buried under snow, they retrieve the right nut at the right time with startling accuracy — not because they remember every hole, but because they remembered the system.

Here's the part that stops people: none of that gathering happens in winter. It can't. By the time snow is falling, the window has already closed. Every calorie a squirrel eats in February was a decision made in October, when the trees were still generous and the days were still long enough to work.

Solomon knew this rhythm too, though he was watching sons instead of squirrels. Proverbs 10 opens the book's long middle section — hundreds of short, sharp sayings meant for a young man learning to run a household, a farm, a life. The first verse sets the tone: "A wise son brings joy to his father, but a foolish son brings grief to his mother" (Prov 10:1). Then Solomon moves fast through four short contrasts — wealth versus poverty, hunger versus provision, laziness versus diligence — before landing on the line that gives the whole passage its edge: "He who gathers crops in summer is a prudent son, but he who sleeps during harvest is a disgraceful son" (Prov 10:5).

He who gathers crops in summer is a prudent son, but he who sleeps during harvest is a disgraceful son. — Proverbs 10:5

Picture the scene behind that verse. A Judean farming family. Harvest week arrives — the one narrow stretch when grain is ripe, dry, and ready to be cut before rain or wind ruins it. Every hand is needed. And somewhere in that busy household, one son is asleep. Not sick. Not away. Just asleep, while the one week that mattered most slips past him. Solomon doesn't call him unlucky. He calls him disgraceful — a strong word for what looks, on the surface, like just being tired.

Here's the fresh angle worth sitting with: this isn't really a proverb about hard work for its own sake. Look at the verse right before it. "Lazy hands make for poverty, but diligent hands bring wealth" (Prov 10:4) sounds like a straightforward productivity slogan — until you notice Solomon already undercut it two verses earlier. "Ill-gotten treasures have no lasting value, but righteousness delivers from death" (Prov 10:2). Solomon isn't glorifying wealth. He just told us it doesn't last. So what is he actually praising in the gathering son?

He's praising attention. The prudent son isn't smarter or stronger than his sleeping brother. He's just awake to what season he's in. He notices that summer is for gathering, not lounging — that certain windows in life open, do their work, and close, whether or not you were paying attention. The squirrel doesn't out-muscle winter. It simply refuses to sleep through October.

And this is where the passage turns from practical to something gentler. Notice what sits just before the diligence verses: "The Lord does not let the righteous go hungry, but he thwarts the craving of the wicked" (Prov 10:3). Provision, Solomon says, ultimately comes from God — not from frantic self-reliance. That changes what "gathering" means. It's not fear-driven hoarding, grabbing everything you can because no one else will provide for you. It's trust that shows up as attentiveness. You gather in summer not because you're terrified of winter, but because you believe the season is a gift worth honoring while it's here.

That's good news for anyone who has ever felt behind. Maybe you slept through a season — a marriage that needed tending, a friendship that needed a phone call, a faith that needed feeding — and you're tempted to think the disgrace is permanent. But Solomon's God is the one who "does not let the righteous go hungry." The gospel doesn't wait for you to have a perfect track record of diligence. Christ himself is the one whose righteousness "delivers from death" (Prov 10:2) — not our own harvest record. Grace is what lets a person wake up mid-October and still start gathering.

So here's something to actually do with this. Ask yourself, plainly: what season am I in right now, and am I awake to it? Maybe it's small — a conversation you keep postponing, a habit of prayer you keep meaning to start, a child who is only this age once. You don't need panic. You need attention. The squirrel doesn't bury ten thousand nuts by working harder than every other animal in the forest. It just refuses to let the ripe season pass unnoticed.

Whatever your harvest is this week, don't sleep through it. Gather while it's still summer.
